newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judge rejects Carlos's book ban bid.
newsitem.headline: French judge rejects Carlos's book ban bid.

text.p: Guerrilla mastermind "Carlos the Jackal", held in a Paris jail since his arrest two years ago, lost his bid on Thursday to have a book banned on the grounds that it violated his right to be presumed innocent.

Judge Francine Levon-Guerin rejected an appeal and a demand for 700,000 francs ($140,000) in damages made by the lawyer of the Venezuelan-born Illich Ramirez Sanchez, who had not attended last Tuesday's hearing.

Lawyer Frederic Pariente had argued that the book "Carlos: The Secret Networks of International Terrorism" by journalist Bernard Violet prejudiced chances of a fair trial for Carlos, who was once the world's most wanted guerrilla suspect.

He also alleged that the publication of a photograph of Carlos -- from a fake Yemeni passport used by Carlos in 1991 -- on the front cover violated his client's right to his image, and that several passages in the book violated his private life.
The other side said Carlos was hypocritical, talking of his rights when he had once bragged of killings.
"(Violet) expresses no definitive personal opinion taking as fact the guilt (of Carlos) in the events for which he is being held," the judge said in her ruling.
She said the photograph had been widely published previously in books and newspaper articles. As a journalist, she added, Violet was not bound by laws governing the secrecy of an investigation.

Carlos, spirited from Sudan in 1994, is awaiting trial in a Paris prison. He has been convicted in his absence by a French court and sentenced to life in prison for the 1975 killings of two secret service agents. French law gives him the right to be retried after his capture in Sudan in August 1994.
Carlos's boldest attack was to lead the 1975 kidnapping of 11 OPEC oil ministers from a conference in Vienna.
France accuses him of killing 83 people in a series of attacks mostly in Europe and the Middle East and he is under investigation for four other bombings in France in the 1980s.
